implementation_notes: ActiveRecord realizes Embedded Value with composed_of: the macro adds a reader and a writer for the value object and describes how the value is built from the entity's attributes on load and turned back into attributes on save (composed_of :address, mapping: { address_street: :street, address_city: :city }). The pattern's immutability requirement is enforced by the framework - ActiveRecord freezes any object assigned as a value object, so changing it raises rather than persisting a partial update. Ruby 3.2's Data.define is the natural way to write the value class itself: immutable, with generated equality and pattern-matching support, and no member writers.
code_sketch:
class Customer < ApplicationRecord
  composed_of :balance, class_name: "Money", mapping: { balance: :amount }
  composed_of :address, mapping: { address_street: :street, address_city: :city }
end

customer.address = Address.new("May Street", "Chicago")  # writes both columns
customer.address_street                                   # => "May Street"
Customer.where(address: Address.new("May Street", "Chicago"))  # query by value
pitfalls: Value objects are frozen on assignment, so an in-place mutator on the value class raises at runtime; write value classes with Data.define or without writers.
The mapping order determines the order of the constructor arguments, so reordering the mapping hash silently swaps the value's fields.
allow_nil is false by default: a value whose mapped attributes are all NULL is still instantiated, and setting the value to nil writes nil to every mapped attribute only when allow_nil is set.
